oDatech.nadpis: About the data and how the atlas was made
oDatech.uvod: The atlas is built on open databases put together by linguists from all over the world. Here is where everything comes from, what is certain and what is only an estimate.

p: Each dot is one language. The list of languages comes from Glottolog, an open database of the world's languages run by the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig. The atlas takes everything Glottolog lists as a language and gives a location: {g} languages.
A dot stands where Glottolog places the language, usually in the middle of the area where it is spoken. Even a language spoken all over the world has just one dot, at its home.

Left out are only Glottolog's special bins: bookkeeping entries, languages known only by name and languages we know so little about that they cannot be classified. Esperanto, Interlingua and Interslavic have no dot because they did not arise in any one place; they are still in the list and in search.

There is no sharp line between a language and a dialect, and history and politics often play a part. The atlas follows Glottolog's decisions. That is why Bavarian has a dot but Australian English does not – Glottolog counts it as a variety of English. Dialects are listed on the language card, and searching for one finds its language.

Serbian, Croatian, Bosnian and Montenegrin are very easy to understand for each other's speakers and rest on the same dialect base, Shtokavian. Linguistically they are close standard varieties of one shared language; officially and socially they are separate languages today. Glottolog lists them as one language, Serbo-Croatian, which has a dot on the globe. The atlas also has Serbian and Croatian as separate languages with a greeting, but they have no dot of their own. Hmong, on the other hand, is several languages in Glottolog and one entry in the atlas. That is why the list has {n} entries and the globe {g} dots.

For 163 selected languages the atlas gives a greeting, an approximate pronunciation, a note, the number of speakers and the area of distribution. These are compiled by hand and the notes are fact-checked.
The pronunciation guide is only approximate. Speaker numbers are rounded estimates that include second-language speakers.
The orange area on the globe is drawn by hand and approximate, not measured. There are no open data with exact language boundaries for the whole world.
The Play pronunciation button uses the device's speech synthesis; for some languages the device has no voice.
The illustrations show the typical landscape and vernacular architecture of the region the language comes from. They do not depict particular places.
Vitality: the UNESCO scale (safe to extinct) based on Glottolog data.

Typology (word order, cases, tone, consonant inventory… – 24 features): WALS Online, the World Atlas of Language Structures (Dryer & Haspelmath 2013). WALS describes a sample of about 2,600 languages; the others have no value. For the map some values are merged into groups; the language card always shows the exact WALS value.
Number of sounds: PHOIBLE. Sample text: Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR in Unicode).
Speaker numbers: Wikidata; where missing, an estimate from Unicode CLDR.
Relatives and the family tree: the Glottolog tree, with Glottolog's branch names.
Nothing is made up: if a source has no data, the card does not show it.
Country borders and land come from Natural Earth (simplified, scale 1:110 million). Relief and the sea floor come from Natural Earth and NOAA ETOPO1.

navod.napoveda: Full guide – all features of the atlas
navod.uvod: The atlas shows all 7,967 languages of the world after Glottolog on an interactive globe. This guide describes every feature and how to use it with a mouse, touch or the keyboard.

p: Rotate: drag with the mouse or one finger. Zoom: mouse wheel, pinch with two fingers, the + and − buttons in the bar, or the + and − keys.

Each dot is one language, placed where Glottolog locates it, usually in the middle of the area where it is spoken. Click a dot to open the language card. From 2× zoom, language names are shown next to the dots (switch them off in View).
Clicking a country away from the dots highlights the country and all its languages and shows their number according to Glottolog.
The Whole world button and the Language Atlas logo in the top left return the globe to its initial view.

163 selected languages have a detailed card: an illustration of the region, a greeting with approximate pronunciation and a Play pronunciation button (it uses the device's speech synthesis). Below are the number of speakers, the language family and vitality, and the tabs Note, Vitality, Structure and Relatives.
All other languages have the tabs Overview (distribution, vitality, dialects, sample text), Structure (WALS typology, PHOIBLE sound inventory, documentation) and Relatives.
The Structure tab gives the exact value for each WALS feature; click a feature name to open its typology map.
Arcs on the globe lead from the selected language to its closest relatives. The language family tree line shows its classification in the Glottolog tree.
The chain button copies a link to the language. On a phone the card sits at the bottom of the screen: drag it up to enlarge it, down to shrink or close it.
You can search for a language, a country or a dialect. The cross in the search box clears it.
Sort by language family, alphabetically or by continent. Languages with a detailed card are shown as large tiles, the others below them.

The Language of the Day changes at midnight and always states why it was chosen: either a day associated with that language (see the Calendar of language days) or the journey around the world to the next nearest language. On the European Day of Languages (26 September) all European languages of the atlas are shown instead.
Random language opens the card of a randomly selected language.
Family tree shows the tree of a whole language family after Glottolog. Drag to move, use the wheel or two fingers to zoom, click a branch to focus on it and click a language to select it.
Vitality colours the languages by degree of endangerment on the UNESCO scale and shows a key; click the key to choose which levels to show.
View: automatic rotation, language names, sign languages (all, none or only these), the vitality filter and typology maps.

In View › Typology (WALS) you can choose one of 24 features in five areas (phonology, morphology, word order, clause structure, lexicon). The languages take the colour of their value and a key appears at the bottom right with the number of languages, a description of the feature and a link to the relevant WALS chapter.

After a choice the list closes; Another feature… in the key reopens it. Clicking a value in the key highlights only the languages with that value. WALS describes a sample of about 2,600 languages; the other dots stay grey.

On a language card choose Compare with another language and select the second language on the globe, in the list or by searching. The comparison shows the relationship and the closest common ancestor, shared and differing WALS features, sound inventories and speaker numbers.
Tab moves between controls. One Tab enters the language list; the arrow keys move between tiles, Home and End jump to the start and end, and Enter selects a language.
The + and − keys zoom the globe. Escape closes a window, the card or a panel.

oddily.h: About, sources, contact, guide and calendar
p: At the end of the language list (on a phone, at the end of the page) there is a folded line: About, sources, contact, guide and calendar. Click it to expand it.

Calendar of language days: the days of the year associated with a particular language (language days, public holidays, anniversaries). It opens at the nearest day; click a language to show it on the globe.
About the data: the sources (Glottolog, WALS, PHOIBLE, Wikidata, Unicode CLDR and others), their versions and licences, and why the list has more entries than there are dots on the globe.
Full guide: this text.
Languages with a detailed card (website only): all 163 languages on one page. Each opens as a card; use the arrows to move to the next one.
Contact: comments and corrections to info@atlasjazyku.cz. Below are the data sources and their licences.
In the top right you can switch the interface language (Česky) and the light or dark theme. Your choices are saved.
Search also knows languages constructed for literature and film (such as Quenya or Klingon); they are shown separately from natural languages.
